title: Bobotie
author: Galiema Adams
desc: Mince cooked down with turmeric, masala and chutney, then baked under a thin savoury custard of egg and milk until the top sets golden — the dish most often called South Africa's national one.
longDesc: Bobotie is the country's best-known dish and it belongs to a kitchen that was never credited. The name most likely comes from the Malay bumbu, a curry spice paste, and the Dictionary of South African English records it in print as early as 1870, spelled Babootie. What makes it bobotie rather than a mince bake is the pairing: warm spice and sweetness in the meat, and a plain unsweetened custard poured over it that sets into a lid. There is no cheese and no pastry anywhere near it.
steps: Heat the oil in a pan and add the onion, chilli and garlic. Let them sizzle for a minute or two.
Add the mince and the salt and fry for 10 minutes, breaking it up as it browns.
Once the mince is cooked through, stir in the turmeric and the masala.
Add the chutney, the bay leaves and the water, and simmer for 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 180C and transfer the mince to a greased ovenproof dish, levelling the surface.
Whisk the milk and eggs together in a separate bowl and pour the mixture over the mince. Lay the bay leaves on top if you want them visible.
Bake for 30 minutes, until the custard is set and golden.
chefTips: Level the mince before the custard goes on. An uneven surface means the custard pools in the dips and bakes dry on the high points.
The custard is deliberately thin — two eggs to three quarters of a cup of milk — so it sets as a lid rather than a quiche. Adding more egg gives you a different dish.
Roasted or leaf masala both work; roasted is darker and deeper. Add more than the two tablespoons if you like it stronger.

Many bobotie recipes fold milk-soaked bread into the mince, and dried fruit with it — apricots, raisins. This version uses neither, which gives a looser, more savoury mince. Both are traditional, and households are firm about which one is correct.
It doubles cleanly for a large dish, which is how it is usually cooked.
commonMistakes: Adding the masala before the mince has browned, so the spice steams rather than frying and tastes raw in the finished dish.
Pouring the custard over hot, loose mince, which lets it sink in instead of sitting on top.
Baking it past the point where the custard sets, which turns it rubbery and weepy.
Sweetening the custard. The sweetness belongs in the mince, from the chutney, and the topping is savoury.
storage: Refrigerate up to 3 days. It slices more cleanly cold.
reheating: Cover and warm in a moderate oven. A microwave makes the custard weep.
healthBenefits: Lean mince supplies protein, iron, zinc and B12.
The egg-and-milk topping adds calcium and more protein.
Naturally gluten-free in this version, since no bread goes into the mince.
culturalNote: Bobotie is routinely called South Africa's national dish, and it comes out of the Cape kitchens of enslaved and exiled people brought by the Dutch East India Company from the seventeenth century onward. Those cooks were prized and almost entirely undocumented: the recipes survived, the names of the women who made them did not. That is worth saying whenever the dish is called a national treasure.
